entries.content:
The house my father grew up in is also the house that I grew up in, through age 12. For a while after they married my father and mother lived in their own (rented) house, but soon after I was born they moved back in with his parents. I don’t know the reason, but I assume that, since both my parents worked full-time (when Daddy wasn’t in prison), they could rely on my grandmother to care for me and then, later, my sister. This she did, faithfully and lovingly, and her memory remains a blessing to me and to my sister.

My grandfather was an engineer for the Frisco railroad, and in many respects the railroad dominated my childhood. The freight yard from which he departed on his long runs across the country — the East Thomas Yard — was less than a mile from our house, and Grandma would always take me in her station wagon to drop him off and pick him up. Sometimes, for reasons unknown to me, we would have to drive to Carbon Hill, Alabama to pick him up. (I think crew changes happened there.) On rare occasions his train would rumble slowly into the yard, or depart slowly from it, along a track that ran just a few dozen yards from our house, and when that happened he played a special pattern on his whistle so I would know it was him. When he was disabled by a stroke and forced to retire from the Frisco, a good deal of magic disappeared from my life.

Our house was an old, beat-up, ramshackle thing with peeling wallpaper inside and watermarks on the ceilings, but when I was very young the yard featured a small fishpond and banks of flowers, especially zinnias, which my grandfather loved. He was the one who cared for the place, and after his stroke everything quickly went to pot. The flowers disappeared, and the fishpond was filled with dirt; the pecan trees, though, kept producing nuts, and it was always my job in the fall to scoop the fallen nuts into grocery bags and offer them to our neighbors. (As an adult I was shocked to learn than people paid for pecans.)

We moved out of that house in the summer of 1971, and not long afterward it burned down. My memory is shaky on this point, and there’s no one left to ask, but I believe the house was left empty and someone burned it down for fun.

When I was in Alabama for my mother’s funeral I went back to the site of that old house, and here’s what I saw:

A jungle. That old neighborhood is gone now; most of the lots look like ours, while a few feature small warehouses and machine shops. No houses remain. The only thing that looks just the same is the sand and gravel business on the other side of the railroad tracks:

On weekends we used to climb that fence and play king of the hill — preferably on the sand piles, because when we tumbled down the mountains of gravel we ended up with a good many bruises and cuts and holes in our jeans. (Our parents tolerated the bruises and cuts but not the holes: jeans were hardy with ordinary use, but were expensive.)

Those great piles of sand and gravel lie just to the north of our neighborhood; just to the south is College Hill, where the lovely tree-filled campus of Birmingham-Southern College (BSC) still stands — though the college, alas, has closed. When I was quite small, before I-65 separated East Thomas from College Hill, one could walk up the hill to BSC and then look down on our house, just visible between the pecan trees.

When we left that house we moved to the East Lake neighborhood of Birmingham; my parents lived in their house there until 1992, when the city of Birmingham declared that the area right next to the lake was flood-prone and ordered the removal of the residents and the demolition of the houses. The affected streets had never experienced any flooding, so everyone was mystified by the decision, though at least some residents, including my parents, were happy to get paid for leaving what they believed to be a declining part of town.

Here’s where our house was:

And if you were to turn 180º to view the rest of the neighborhood, this is what you would see:

All those old trees, still providing shade for houses and people who aren’t there any more. (You can just see the outline of sidewalks.) I hope the trees don’t miss us; I fear that the ones at BSC are lonely now, though that may change.

These stories are in many ways characteristic of Birmingham. When I was born the city had nearly 400,000 people; now it has fewer than 200,000. Most of those who have departed (like my parents) were white: in 1960 the population of Birmingham was 60% white, while now the figure is closer to 25%. The departed were not replaced, thus the empty or demolished houses — and schools also: the first school I attended, Gorgas Elementary, was demolished decades ago; the next, Elyton School has been abandoned; and Banks High School was first abandoned and then demolished. I don’t know about Gorgas or Elyton, but the explicit reason for the closing of Banks High School was declining enrollments: the neighborhoods around the school were slowly depopulating.

It’s a familiar story, quite a bit like that of a larger industrial city, Detroit. Birmingham’s central downtown, where many people still work, features high-level restaurants and bars and nice hotels, but outside the downtown area is a large Ring of Abandonment, and beyond that you find bustling, prosperous suburbs. (The actual city of Birmingham may hold 190,000 people, but the metropolitan area holds a million and a quarter.) A few days ago I was enjoying the best pizza I have ever had in my life — and I’ve eaten a lot of great pizza, in Italy and elsewhere — at Pizza Grace and reflecting that probably none of the other patrons in this wonderful downtown restaurant live in Birmingham: they almost certainly live in Mountain Brook and Vestavia and Hoover and maybe Trussville, though they may well work in the city.

So, a familiar story, the way of the world; but it’s odd and somewhat disorienting, especially in this season of my life, in which I have just buried my mother, to realize that I can revisit none of the foundational places of my life. They’re all gone.

entries.content:
Yesterday we buried my mother in Hopewell Cemetery, Hanceville, Alabama. She lies next to her husband, Carl Edwin Jacobs, who died in 2009 on their fifty-fifth wedding anniversary. Next to them are the graves of my father’s parents, Elisha Creel Jacobs (1902-1971) and Margaret Doran Jacobs (1909-1997).

But why are they all here? Not one of them ever lived a day in Hanceville, and each of them died in Birmingham, where they spent most of their lives.

The answer may be found on a small stone on the opposite side of my grandparents’ graves from my parents’ graves:

Bobby Jacobs — more formally Robert Alan Jacobs — was the second son of Elisha and Margaret, born nineteen months after Carl. I am named for this uncle I never knew, but with the first and middle names reversed. Bobby was born with a club foot and could never walk properly; my father, who early on assumed the role of Bobby’s chief caregiver, used to pull him around the neighborhood in a wagon. But the club foot was only the first of Bobby’s misfortunes; later he contracted polio and died, a few weeks shy of his sixth birthday.

Immediately after Bobby took his last breath, Carl, then seven years old, did a peculiar thing: he ran straight to the tallest pecan tree in his yard and climbed to the highest branch that would bear him, where he clung, weeping. He remained perched there for hours and hours; no one could talk him down, until, as night fell, someone finally fetched the local Baptist minister, whose authority, maybe, was sufficient to compel Carl to return to the land of the living — and the dead. Or maybe the boy was just worn out.

At the time of Bobby’s death, my grandmother was pregnant with her third child, to be born the following year: Elisha Creel Jacobs, Jr. My father occasionally reminded me that “After Bobby died, your grandmother took to her bed for two years and didn’t lift a goddamn finger.” He despised his mother and, probably because I loved her so intensely, wanted me to despise her too, so when he said this he never mentioned that during those two years, after having lost one child, she had to bear another. Though they didn’t use the word “depression” in those days, much less “postpartum depression,” she must have been profoundly depressed, and that shouldn’t have been difficult for anyone to understand.

There’s much I could say about my father, not all of it bad, and I will acknowledge some of the better things on another occasion, but at the moment I am compelled to state that for much of his life he was a shockingly cruel man. When his younger brother E.C. died, in 2000, and E.C.’s ex-wife called my father to give him the news, my father replied “I don’t give a shit” and hung up the phone. I don’t know where this cruelty came from, but I have a strange but persistent intuition that it originated with Bobby’s death — or, rather, emerged in that moment, immediately after Bobby’s death, when instead of grieving with his mother and father he chose to climb that tree and grieve alone, holding his misery as fiercely as he gripped the swaying branch that kept him aloft, high above the human world. This is, I suspect, why even as an old man he was intolerant of his mother’s sorrow at the loss of that same child, the child that she had borne in her own body. It’s my grief, he seemed to say, not ours — and certainly not yours.

My grandfather had many siblings, but the one to whom he was closest, both emotionally and geographically, was the woman we called Aunt B: Bethelee Jacobs Basenberg. She was sixteen years older than my grandfather and I think she must have been a kind of mother to him. (His own mother, when Bobby died, was living in Mississippi, at a time when such distances were harder to bridge. For instance, no one in my family then had telephones, and the roads were often poor. Many of my rural and small-town relatives may not have had electricity in 1934.) I knew her much later, of course, but I remember her vividly: a grand old matriarch who, long after the passing of her husband Mart, still ran their farm. She grew corn mostly, but also had a kitchen garden where she nurtured strawberries and sugar cane, and when we visited she would send me away with grocery bags full of both. One of the vividest memories of my childhood involves sitting at our kitchen table at home and squeezing syrup from her canes over a bowl of her strawberries.

Aunt B’s farm was just outside Hanceville, where she was for many decades a devoted member of Hopewell Baptist Church. Indeed, she is buried in the same cemetery, a few yards from her younger brother, who outlived her by a mere two months.

And now I think we can, with some confidence, piece the story together. When Bobby died, Elisha and Margaret must have turned to Bethelee, that sheet anchor and faithful Christian — they themselves were never more than intermittent churchgoers, nor were their children later — and she must have taken charge of the situation, bringing her nephew’s body to the graveyard next to the church where she worshipped every week. That tiny rectangle with its awkwardly formed epitaph was all that they could afford then, in the depths of the Great Depression, but at least she could watch over the boy’s grave and make sure it was graced with flowers, probably flowers from her own garden.

And then, in time, the rest of the family came to their repose at the same spot — all except poor E.C., the favorite uncle of my youth, whose place of burial, thanks to my father’s mean indifference, remains unknown to me, though I have searched for it. E.C. was a man of many sins and many sorrows, and perhaps some day I will be able to give him, too, a proper tribute.

At the moment, though, I am thinking of the raw red dirt that now marks my mother’s grave, a grave soon to be covered with grass, like the others, all but one of which feature dignified upright tombstones. The larger picture: In the middle, my grandmother and grandfather; to one side of them their eldest son Carl and his wife Dolores; to the other side the child whose death initiated this story, a little boy, misshapen in body and then racked by a vile disease, whose brief life is now marked by a chunk of rock invisible except to the attentive — a little boy who was greatly, greatly cherished, and whose death brought lasting misery to his family.

My father used to say, sneeringly, “Oh, when you were born, Mama thought she had Bobby back, had Bobby all over again.” But Daddy, if you didn’t want her to feel that way, why did you give me his name? You couldn’t have “Bobby all over again” only for yourself.

As I say, we buried my mother yesterday, and to my family I read the beautiful and consoling words of the Book of Common Prayer: “O God, who by the glorious resurrection of your Son Jesus Christ destroyed death, and brought life and immortality to light: Grant that your servant Dolores, being raised with him, may know the strength of his presence, and rejoice in his eternal glory … In sure and certain hope of the resurrection to eternal life through our Lord Jesus Christ, we commend to Almighty God our mother Dolores, and we commit her body to the ground; earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust. The Lord bless her and keep her; the Lord make his face to shine upon her and be gracious to her; the Lord lift up his countenance upon her and give her peace. Amen.”

But for some reason — perhaps because I have been grieving my mother’s death for some time already — it’s Bobby I am thinking of today. My father lived eighty-two years, my mother ninety-four; Bobby never made it to age six. Now, of course, those gathered in that little country churchyard “accept the constitution of silence / And are folded in a single party.” May light perpetual shine upon them all.
